```{python}
#| output: false
import subprocess, io, os, sys, glob, json, tomllib
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.getcwd(), ".."))
from _lib.cli import run_cli

GREY = "#888888"
mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": "none", "axes.facecolor": "none",
    "savefig.facecolor": "none", "figure.dpi": 150, "font.size": 11,
    "text.color": GREY, "axes.labelcolor": GREY,
    "xtick.color": GREY, "ytick.color": GREY,
    "axes.edgecolor": GREY, "legend.edgecolor": GREY,
})

VDIR = "he2010-v0"
MODEL = os.path.join(VDIR, "models/he2010_london.camdl")
PARAMS = os.path.join(VDIR, "params/he2010_london.toml")
SYNTH_OBS = os.path.join(VDIR, "data/he2010_synthetic_obs.tsv")

# Pre-computed pomp reference ensemble (200 sims at He et al. MLE),
# generated by ../../../camdl-vignettes/he2010-forward/bench/pomp/01_pomp_reference.R
POMP_ENSEMBLE = os.path.join(
    "..", "..", "camdl-vignettes", "he2010-forward",
    "bench", "pomp", "out", "pomp_ensemble.tsv",
)

def simulate_weekly(seed: int = 42) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Run camdl and return weekly_cases with time column."""
    outfile = f"/tmp/hesyn_{os.getpid()}_{seed}.tsv"
    subprocess.run(
        ["camdl", "simulate", MODEL, "--params", PARAMS,
         "--backend", "chain_binomial", "--dt", "1",
         "--seed", str(seed), "--obs-only", outfile],
        check=True, capture_output=True, text=True,
    )
    df = pl.read_csv(outfile, separator="\t", comment_prefix="#")
    os.remove(outfile)
    return df
```

Before fitting the He et al. model to real London measles data, we
validate the inference pipeline on synthetic data where the true
parameters are known. This is the essential *"can we recover what we
put in?"* check — if IF2 can't find the truth on synthetic data, fitting
real data is meaningless.

Before even that: we need to trust the forward simulator. If camdl's
implementation of the model diverges from its specification — from
the pomp reference, from He et al.'s paper — then the "truth" we simulate
to generate synthetic data is not the truth we think it is. Two silent
unit bugs ([camdl#11](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl/issues/11)) made
this not hypothetical: before their fix, camdl's forward simulator at
He et al.'s MLE produced extinction in every realization, while pomp
produced persistent measles in every realization. The chapter's current
analysis is performed on the post-fix runtime, and the forward-simulation
validation below is the precondition that authorizes the recovery test
that follows.


## Forward-simulation validation: camdl vs. pomp

pomp ([King, Nguyen, and Ionides 2016](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v069.i12))
is the canonical reference implementation of He et al.'s model.
[`vignettes/he2010-v0/validation/envelope_smoke.py`](../he2010-v0/validation/README.md)
runs 200 camdl forward simulations at the He et al. MLE and compares
ensemble statistics to a 200-sim pomp reference. After the
[camdl#11](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl/issues/11) fixes, camdl's
median agrees with pomp to < 1% on total cases and peak-per-epidemic.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Stochastic envelope: 200 camdl simulations (blue ribbon = 5–95% quantiles, line = median) vs. 200 pomp simulations (grey dashed). Observed London 1944–1965 data in red for scale. At the He et al. MLE the two implementations produce indistinguishable envelopes. The real data (red) lies inside the envelope — i.e. it is a plausible draw from the fitted model."
#| label: fig-envelope
#| fig-height: 4.5

# --- camdl ensemble (compute if cache missing; else reuse) ---
CACHE = os.path.join(VDIR, "validation", "camdl_ensemble_cache.tsv")
if os.path.exists(CACHE):
    camdl_wide = pl.read_csv(CACHE, separator="\t")
else:
    rows = []
    for seed in range(1, 201):
        df = simulate_weekly(seed=seed)
        rows.append(df["weekly_cases"].to_numpy())
    T = min(len(r) for r in rows)
    arr = np.array([r[:T] for r in rows]).T  # (T, n_sims)
    times = simulate_weekly(seed=1)["time"].to_numpy()[:T]
    cols = {"time": times}
    for i, s in enumerate(range(1, 201)):
        cols[f"sim_{s}"] = arr[:, i]
    camdl_wide = pl.DataFrame(cols)
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(CACHE), exist_ok=True)
    camdl_wide.write_csv(CACHE, separator="\t")

camdl_arr = camdl_wide.drop("time").to_numpy()
camdl_t = camdl_wide["time"].to_numpy() / 365.25
camdl_q05 = np.percentile(camdl_arr, 5, axis=1)
camdl_q50 = np.percentile(camdl_arr, 50, axis=1)
camdl_q95 = np.percentile(camdl_arr, 95, axis=1)

# --- pomp ensemble ---
pomp_raw = pl.read_csv(
    POMP_ENSEMBLE, separator="\t",
    schema_overrides={"S": pl.Float64, "E": pl.Float64, "I": pl.Float64,
                      "R": pl.Float64, "C": pl.Float64, "t_days": pl.Float64})
# Pivot to wide: rows=time, cols=sim
pomp_wide = pomp_raw.pivot(values="cases", index="t_days", on="sim").sort("t_days")
pomp_t = pomp_wide["t_days"].to_numpy() / 365.25
pomp_arr = pomp_wide.drop("t_days").to_numpy()
pomp_q05 = np.percentile(pomp_arr, 5, axis=1)
pomp_q50 = np.percentile(pomp_arr, 50, axis=1)
pomp_q95 = np.percentile(pomp_arr, 95, axis=1)

# --- real data ---
real = pl.read_csv(os.path.join(VDIR, "data", "he2010_london_cases.tsv"),
                    separator="\t")
real_t = real["time"].to_numpy() / 365.25
real_cases = real["cases"].to_numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.5))
ax.fill_between(camdl_t, camdl_q05, camdl_q95, color="#3366cc", alpha=0.25,
                linewidth=0, label="camdl 5–95%")
ax.plot(camdl_t, camdl_q50, color="#1e3a8a", linewidth=0.9,
        label="camdl median")
ax.plot(pomp_t, pomp_q50, color=GREY, linewidth=0.9, linestyle="--",
        label="pomp median")
ax.plot(pomp_t, pomp_q05, color=GREY, linewidth=0.4, linestyle=":",
        alpha=0.7)
ax.plot(pomp_t, pomp_q95, color=GREY, linewidth=0.4, linestyle=":",
        alpha=0.7, label="pomp 5 / 95%")
ax.plot(real_t, real_cases, color="#cc3333", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.9,
        label="London 1944–1965")
ax.set_xlabel("Years since 1944-01-07")
ax.set_ylabel("Weekly cases")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper right")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This is the figure that would have caught [camdl#11](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl/issues/11)
during authoring. Before the fix, the blue ribbon would have collapsed to
near-zero after year 2 while the grey (pomp) ribbon persisted — an
impossible-to-miss visual indictment of the implementation. A
distributional smoke test
([`validation/envelope_smoke.py`](../he2010-v0/validation/README.md))
now runs this check automatically with five regression thresholds
calibrated to the post-fix agreement level (median total within 10% of
pomp, etc.).


## The synthetic dataset

We simulate 21 years of weekly measles notifications at the He et al.
MLE (`seed = 42`) and treat the output as our "observed" synthetic data.
Because it's a single draw from a stochastic DGP, it's one realization
among many; the envelope figure above shows the distribution of
realizations the same parameters can produce.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic measles data used for the recovery test: 21 years of weekly notifications, seed 42, drawn from the model at the He et al. MLE. The recurrent-epidemic pattern is characteristic of measles in large pre-vaccination populations. This one realization is what the IF2 scout sees as 'the data'; the recovery test asks whether IF2 can back out the parameters that generated it."
#| label: fig-synthetic-data
#| fig-height: 3.5

obs = pl.read_csv(SYNTH_OBS, separator="\t")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.fill_between(obs["time"] / 365.25, 0, obs["weekly_cases"],
                color="#cc3333", alpha=0.2, linewidth=0)
ax.plot(obs["time"] / 365.25, obs["weekly_cases"], color="#cc3333",
        linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.85)
ax.set_xlabel("Years")
ax.set_ylabel("Weekly cases")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## Data leakage in synthetic validation

It is tempting, when generating synthetic data for a recovery test, to
filter stochastic realizations based on whether they "look like" the real
data — keep only seeds whose peak heights, biennial phase, or total-case
count resemble the target. **Do not.** This is data leakage: the real
dataset is informing which draws you accept, so the recovery test is no
longer evaluating inference on an independent stochastic realization —
it is evaluating inference on a realization pre-selected to resemble the
data it will be compared against. Your "recovery" is circular.

The sharpest rule: **the rejection criterion for synthetic draws must be
definable without reference to the specific real dataset.** Criteria
that are safe: the simulation did not go extinct; compartment counts are
non-negative; the trajectory respects structural properties of the model
class (measles is *supposed to* have recurrent dynamics in a large
enough population). Criteria that cook the books: peak cases within a
factor of 2 of the real data, correlation with the real time series
above a threshold, match to London's specific biennial phase or trough
timings.

In this chapter, the synthetic dataset is a single unfiltered draw from
`seed = 42`. No rejection, no curation. The forward-simulation
validation above (camdl vs. pomp ensemble agreement) is a *system*
property — we are checking that camdl's runtime matches its specified
model, not that camdl's output matches London's data — so it does not
leak.

Data leakage in validation is subtle and pernicious because it often
produces apparently clean recovery results — the inference "works"
because you accidentally arranged for it to work. Catching it requires
asking, at every filtering step, *would this criterion have changed if I
had never seen the real data?* If the answer is no, the criterion is
safe. If it is yes, it is leakage.
:::


## True parameters

The parameters we're trying to recover:

| Parameter | Symbol | True value | Description |
|-----------|--------|------------|-------------|
| R₀ | `R0` | 56.8 | Basic reproduction number |
| σ | `sigma` | 0.0791 | Latent rate (1/σ ≈ 12.6 days) |
| γ | `gamma` | 0.0832 | Recovery rate (1/γ ≈ 12.0 days) |
| Amplitude | `amplitude` | 0.554 | School-term forcing amplitude |
| α | `alpha` | 0.976 | Mixing exponent |
| s₀ | `s0` | 0.0297 | Initial susceptible fraction |

Six parameters estimated; nine fixed at truth (μ, ι, σ_se, cohort, ρ, ψ,
e₀, i₀, N₀). This is the same setup as He et al.'s original IF2
procedure.


## IF2 scout

The scout stage explores the parameter space with 36 dispersed chains,
each running 200 IF2 iterations with 2000 particles:

### Scout results

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
TRUE_PARAMS = {
    "R0": 56.8, "sigma": 0.0791, "gamma": 0.0832,
    "amplitude": 0.554, "alpha": 0.976, "s0": 0.0297,
}

def _populated_scouts_by_mtime():
    matches = glob.glob(os.path.join(
        VDIR, "results/fits/fit_synthetic-*/real/fit_42/scout"))
    populated = [p for p in matches
                 if os.path.exists(os.path.join(p, "fit_state.toml"))]
    populated.sort(key=lambda p: os.path.getmtime(
        os.path.join(p, "fit_state.toml")))
    return populated

def _latest_scout_dir():
    """The most recent populated scout (widened s0 bounds — see the fit config above)."""
    scouts = _populated_scouts_by_mtime()
    return scouts[-1] if scouts else None

SCOUT_DIR = _latest_scout_dir()
scout_populated = (SCOUT_DIR is not None
                   and os.path.exists(os.path.join(SCOUT_DIR, "fit_state.toml")))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if scout_populated:
    # Load scout's chain traces, state, MLE
    traces = []
    chain_dirs = [p for p in glob.glob(os.path.join(SCOUT_DIR, "chain_*"))
                   if os.path.isdir(p)]
    for cdir in sorted(chain_dirs,
                        key=lambda p: int(os.path.basename(p).split("_")[1])):
        trace_path = os.path.join(cdir, "parameter_traces.tsv")
        with open(trace_path) as f:
            tsv_lines = [l for l in f if not l.startswith("#")]
        df = pl.read_csv(io.StringIO("".join(tsv_lines)),
                         separator="\t", infer_schema_length=10000)
        cid = int(os.path.basename(cdir).split("_")[1])
        df = df.with_columns(pl.lit(cid).alias("chain"))
        traces.append(df)
    traces_df = pl.concat(traces) if traces else None
    with open(os.path.join(SCOUT_DIR, "fit_state.toml"), "rb") as f:
        state = tomllib.load(f)
    chain_lls = state.get("chain_logliks", [])
    agreements = state.get("tail_chain_agreement", {})
    best_ll = state.get("best_loglik", float("nan"))
    with open(os.path.join(SCOUT_DIR, "mle_params.toml"), "rb") as f:
        mle_raw = tomllib.load(f)
else:
    traces_df = None
    chain_lls, agreements, mle_raw = [], {}, {}
```

#| output: asis
if scout_populated and mle_raw and agreements:
    params = ["R0", "sigma", "gamma", "amplitude", "alpha", "s0"]

    print("|-----------|-------|------------------|------|---------|--------|")

        elif agreement < 1.05 and pct_err < 20:
            status = "✓ converged + near-truth"
        elif agreement < 1.05:
            status = "⚠ converged but biased"
        elif agreement < 1.10:
            status = "~ marginal"
        else:
            status = "✗ not converged"
        print(f"| `{p}` | {truth:.4g} | {mle:.4g} | {agreement:.3f} "
              f"| {pct_err:.1f}% | {status} |")

#| fig-cap: "Pair plot of the wider-bounds rerun, same conventions as the earlier figure. Key visual test: does s0 (bottom-right diagonal) still show the double-peak at bounds? If it does, the problem is deeper than bound geometry. If it resolves to a unimodal cluster near truth (0.03), the narrow-bounds scout above was trapped procedurally and refine can now proceed."

if scout_populated and traces_df is not None:
    params = ["R0", "sigma", "gamma", "amplitude", "alpha", "s0"]
    N_LAST = 60
    max_iter = int(traces_df["iteration"].max())
    tail_df = traces_df.filter(pl.col("iteration") > max_iter - N_LAST)

    endpoints_rows = []
    for cid in sorted(traces_df["chain"].unique()):
        fp_path = os.path.join(SCOUT_DIR, f"chain_{cid}", "final_params.toml")
        if not os.path.exists(fp_path):
            continue
        with open(fp_path, "rb") as f:
            fp = tomllib.load(f)
        row = {"chain": int(cid)}

            row[p] = fp.get(p, float("nan"))
        endpoints_rows.append(row)
    endpoints = pl.DataFrame(endpoints_rows).sort("chain")

    chain_ll_map = {cid: ll for cid, ll in enumerate(chain_lls, start=1)}
    best_ll = max(chain_lls)

    def _basin(ll):
        if ll > best_ll - 500:   return 0
        if ll > best_ll - 2000:  return 1
        if ll > best_ll - 6000:  return 2
        return 3

    basin_colors = {0: "#1e3a8a", 1: "#f59e0b", 2: "#9333ea", 3: "#cc3333"}
    basin_labels = {0: "best (<500 nats)", 1: "middle (500–2000)",
                    2: "middle (2000–6000)", 3: "worst (>6000)"}

    tail_rows = tail_df.to_dicts()
    tail_basin = np.array([_basin(chain_ll_map[r["chain"]]) for r in tail_rows])
    tail_arr = {p: np.array([r[p] for r in tail_rows]) for p in params}

    ep_basin = [_basin(chain_ll_map[c]) for c in endpoints["chain"].to_list()]
    ep_x = {p: endpoints[p].to_numpy() for p in params}

    n = len(params)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n, n, figsize=(13, 10))
    for i, py in enumerate(params):
        for j, px in enumerate(params):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            if i == j:
                for b in sorted(set(tail_basin)):
                    vals = tail_arr[py][tail_basin == b]
                    if len(vals):
                        ax.hist(vals, bins=25, color=basin_colors[b],
                                alpha=0.55, edgecolor="none")
                ax.axvline(TRUE_PARAMS[py], color="black", linewidth=1.2,
                           linestyle="--", alpha=0.85)
                ax.set_yticks([])
            else:
                for b in sorted(set(tail_basin)):
                    m = tail_basin == b
                    if m.any():
                        ax.scatter(tail_arr[px][m], tail_arr[py][m],
                                   color=basin_colors[b], alpha=0.22,
                                   s=5, linewidth=0)
                for b in sorted(set(ep_basin)):
                    mask = [k for k in range(len(ep_basin)) if ep_basin[k] == b]
                    if mask:
                        ax.scatter([ep_x[px][k] for k in mask],
                                   [ep_x[py][k] for k in mask],
                                   facecolors="none", edgecolors=basin_colors[b],
                                   s=60, linewidth=1.2, zorder=6)
                ax.scatter(TRUE_PARAMS[px], TRUE_PARAMS[py],
                           marker="x", color="black", s=90, linewidth=2.2,
                           zorder=10)
            if i == n - 1: ax.set_xlabel(px, fontsize=10)
            else:          ax.set_xticklabels([])
            if j == 0:     ax.set_ylabel(py, fontsize=10)
            else:          ax.set_yticklabels([])
            ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
            ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    handles = [plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w",
                          markerfacecolor=basin_colors[b], markersize=8,
                          label=basin_labels[b])
               for b in sorted(set(ep_basin))]
    handles.append(plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w",
                               markerfacecolor="none", markeredgecolor="black",
                               markeredgewidth=1.2, markersize=9,
                               label="per-chain MLE"))
    handles.append(plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="x", color="black",
                               linewidth=0, markersize=9, label="truth"))
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="center left",
                bbox_to_anchor=(0.82, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=10,
                title="basin", title_fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 0.80, 1))
    plt.show()

## Posterior-predictive check: does the scout MLE match the data?

The recovery table above shows the scout's MLE is biased from truth on
most parameters, and the pair plot shows that bias reflects the scout
sitting in a wrong basin. The direct test of what that means for the
forward-generative model is to simulate from the reported MLE and
overlay against the observed synthetic data. A well-calibrated MLE
should produce an envelope that contains the data; a wrong-basin MLE
should produce trajectories that are visibly off.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Posterior-predictive envelope from the scout MLE: 100 stochastic realizations from the best-chain MLE, vs. the observed synthetic data (red). If the ridge-trapped MLE still reproduces the data envelope, the ridge is likelihood-flat — the MLE is 'wrong' only in the sense that the ridge accommodates many equivalent fits. If the envelope does NOT cover the data at epidemic peaks, the scout found a genuinely worse optimum; the data is discriminating and IF2 failed to reach the good basin."
#| label: fig-ppc
#| fig-height: 4.5

def sim_ensemble(mle_path, n_sims=100):
    """Run n_sims at the given MLE param file, return weekly_cases matrix."""
    sims = []
    for seed in range(1, n_sims + 1):
        outfile = f"/tmp/ppc_{os.getpid()}_{seed}.tsv"
        subprocess.run(
            ["camdl", "simulate", MODEL, "--params", mle_path,
             "--backend", "chain_binomial", "--dt", "1",
             "--seed", str(seed), "--obs-only", outfile],
            check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
        df = pl.read_csv(outfile, separator="\t", comment_prefix="#")
        os.remove(outfile)
        sims.append(df["weekly_cases"].to_numpy())
    T = min(len(s) for s in sims)
    return np.array([s[:T] for s in sims]).T, df["time"].to_numpy()[:T] / 365.25

MLE_PATH = os.path.join(SCOUT_DIR, "mle_params.toml")

obs = pl.read_csv(SYNTH_OBS, separator="\t")
obs_t = obs["time"].to_numpy() / 365.25
obs_cases = obs["weekly_cases"].to_numpy()

arr, tt = sim_ensemble(MLE_PATH, n_sims=100)
q05 = np.percentile(arr, 5, axis=1)
q50 = np.percentile(arr, 50, axis=1)
q95 = np.percentile(arr, 95, axis=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.5))
ax.fill_between(tt, q05, q95, color="#9333ea", alpha=0.25, linewidth=0,
                label="MLE envelope 5–95%")
ax.plot(tt, q50, color="#9333ea", linewidth=0.9, label="MLE median")
ax.plot(obs_t, obs_cases, color="#cc3333", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.85,
        label="synthetic obs (truth)")
ax.set_xlabel("Years")
ax.set_ylabel("Weekly cases")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper right")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```



## Profile likelihood over s0

Direct test of whether s0 is identifiable. We did this two ways, and
the comparison itself teaches something.

The **slice likelihood** below fixes s0 at grid values, holds the other
five parameters at a reference point (either truth, or the scout MLE),
and evaluates the PF log-likelihood at each grid point — a 1D slice of
the 6D likelihood surface along the s0 axis. Cheap but with a known
pathology: at grid points where the fixed reference parameters don't
accommodate the varied s0 (e.g., truth's R0 with a larger s0 forces an
over-sized first epidemic), the PF impoverishes.

The **profile likelihood** further below does the statistically correct
thing: at each s0 grid point it re-optimizes all five other parameters
via IF2, reporting the conditional maximum log-likelihood and the
conditional MLE of each compensating parameter. More expensive per
grid point, but immune to the PF-impoverishment pathology — at each
point the other parameters adapt to keep the simulated trajectory
consistent with the data, so the PF doesn't have to struggle across
a model-data mismatch. This is what you actually want if you care
about whether the parameter is identifiable by the data.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Slice vs. profile: numerical behavior, not just conceptual purity

The textbook reason to prefer a profile likelihood over a slice is
statistical: the profile is the *conditional maximum* given the grid
value, so peaks, curvature, and identifiability conclusions transfer to
the full likelihood surface. The slice conditions on a single arbitrary
point and can't.

A secondary reason, relevant in practice and visible in this chapter's
own numbers: **the profile is usually better-behaved numerically at the
same particle count**. Our 4k-particle slice (on the truth reference)
plunged into a PF-impoverishment dip from ll ≈ −6000 down to ll ≈
−11,000 at s0 ∈ [0.032, 0.048]. The mechanism is exactly what the
conditional-MLE interpretation predicts: at those slice grid points
we're evaluating the likelihood of a mis-specified model (too-large
initial susceptibles with truth's R0) against the data, which produces
trajectories the PF can't reconcile with observations. At the same 4k
particle count, a **profile** likelihood avoids this entirely —
because its other-parameter MLEs adapt to keep the model data-consistent
at every grid point. The bill for "I used a slice to save compute"
comes due as PF impoverishment that requires 4× more particles to
paper over. You can pay it up-front in optimization cost (profile) or
later in particle count (slice); the profile is usually the better
deal, and crucially is the only one whose peaks you can trust
asymptotically.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## Reading a particle-filter profile: impoverishment vs. structure

The profile below shows a conspicuous drop in the truth-slice (blue) at
s0 ∈ [0.032, 0.048] — a region just *above* truth — from ll ≈ −6000 at
truth down to ll ≈ −11,000 and back. **This is not a feature of the
underlying likelihood.** It is **particle-filter impoverishment**: the
4000-particle bootstrap filter collapses in regions where the model
over-predicts the observed data.

The mechanism: at truth values for the other parameters, the model is
tuned to produce the observed synthetic data. Bumping s0 slightly up
(more initial susceptibles) makes the simulated first epidemic *overshoot*
the observed one. Most particles end up on trajectories inconsistent with
the data; the filter resamples heavily onto the few "lucky" particles
that happened to produce smaller trajectories; effective sample size
collapses; the log-likelihood estimate plunges. The true underlying
log-likelihood almost certainly passes smoothly through this region.

Three diagnostic tells that a PF drop is impoverishment, not structure:

- **All replicates at the dip grid point collapse together.** At
  s0 = 0.0322 (just above truth), replicate SD is 463 nats — vs. 2 nats
  at the nearby truth grid point. High per-replicate variance in a
  specific region is the signature.
- **The dip is narrow and recovers.** At s0 = 0.048, the PF stabilizes
  again at a degraded-but-self-consistent ll ≈ −6100. Real likelihood
  features don't recover like that; PF "modes" do.
- **The dip is asymmetric between slices.** The MLE slice (red) has no
  equivalent dip in the same s0 region, because at MLE other-params the
  model under-predicts rather than over-predicts — so bumping s0 up just
  fills capacity the model was short on.

The mitigation is **more particles, not more replicates**. Replicates
average out Monte Carlo noise but don't fix systematic degeneracy. At
16,000 particles (4× more) the dip is empirically confirmed to flatten
(see the 16k overlay in the figure below): the log-likelihood in the
dip region rises by ~5000 nats back to −6000, and per-replicate SD
drops from 200–800 nats to < 2 nats. The true likelihood surface is
smooth; the 4k dip was a 100%-artifact of particle-filter impoverishment
at insufficient particle count.

We keep the 4000-particle curve in the figure as a didactic example —
this is what real PF profiles look like in the field and you will
encounter them — with the 16k-particle curve overlaid to show what
"enough particles" fixes.
:::

```{python}

Shaded bands are ±1 Monte Carlo SD across replicates. Vertical lines: truth (s0 = 0.0297) and the scout MLE. At 16k the truth slice is smooth and unimodal with a clear peak at truth; the 4k dip is entirely a PF-estimation artifact, not a likelihood feature. was a slicing artifact, not a feature of the likelihood surface.

conditional optimum), and **γ** (recovery rate, moderately coupled

## Why is s0 unidentifiable? An analytical derivation

The profile figure above shows a flat log-likelihood across a factor of
~30 in s0 while α compensates monotonically — the signature of a
one-dimensional identifiability ridge. We can derive the ridge direction
from the model's force-of-infection expression, compare the prediction
to the profile data, and arrive at a formal Fisher-singularity
statement.

### Setup

The per-susceptible force of infection in the He et al. model is

$$\lambda(t) \;=\; \beta(t) \cdot \frac{(I(t) + \iota)^\alpha}{N(t)},
\qquad \beta(t) = R_0 \cdot \mathrm{seas}(t) \cdot (\gamma + \mu).$$

During the early phase of the first epidemic, before susceptible
depletion, the rate of new infections is

$$\text{rate}(S \to E) \;\approx\;
\beta \cdot s_0 \cdot N \cdot \frac{(I + \iota)^\alpha}{N}
\;=\; \beta \cdot s_0 \cdot (I + \iota)^\alpha.$$

For the epidemic phase, $I$ is dominated by $I_0 = i_0 \cdot N \approx 127$
or by its peak value $\sim 10^3$–$10^4$, both much larger than
$\iota = 2.9$. Drop $\iota$ for the ridge analysis (it re-enters only in
troughs, which don't dominate the likelihood):

$$\text{rate}(S \to E) \;\approx\; \beta \cdot s_0 \cdot I^\alpha.$$

### The ridge direction

Take logs:

$$\log \text{rate} \;=\; \log \beta \;+\; \log s_0 \;+\; \alpha \log I.$$

The likelihood depends on how well the simulated rate trajectory matches
the observations. Two parameter settings $(s_0, \alpha)$ that produce
the same effective rate at a characteristic $I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ produce the
same likelihood (to leading order, over the relevant time window).

Setting $\log s_0 + \alpha \log I_{\mathrm{ref}} = \mathrm{const}$ and
differentiating along the ridge:

$$\boxed{\frac{d(\log s_0)}{d \alpha} \;=\; -\log I_{\mathrm{ref}}.}$$

The ridge in $(\log s_0, \alpha)$-space is a straight line with slope
$-\log I_{\mathrm{ref}}$. A linear slope in semi-log space is exactly what
the profile's α panel should trace if the analysis is correct.

### Fisher-information interpretation

The Fisher information matrix has, along the ridge direction,

$$H_{\mathrm{ridge}} \;\propto\;
\int \left(
  \frac{\partial \log \text{rate}}{\partial \alpha}
  \;+\;
  \frac{\partial \log \text{rate}}{\partial \log s_0}
  \cdot \frac{d \log s_0}{d \alpha}
\right)^{\!2} dt \;=\; 0$$

by construction: the two terms cancel exactly along the constant-rate
ridge. The curvature perpendicular to the ridge is nonzero (moving off
the ridge changes the likelihood), but *along* the ridge the information
is zero. This is formal non-identifiability in the Rothenberg/Fisher
sense: the information matrix is singular, the Cramér–Rao bound is
infinite, and no finite amount of data can resolve $s_0$ and $\alpha$
independently — only their ridge-aligned combination
$\kappa \equiv s_0 \cdot I_{\mathrm{ref}}^\alpha$ is identified.

### Comparing theory to the profile data

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Empirical identifiability ridge: α vs log₁₀(s0) at the conditional MLE of each profile grid point. Black line is the theoretical ridge slope from the FOI derivation (fit to the upper-s0 portion where the ridge is active). Colored dots are the conditional MLEs across the profile; dot size is proportional to exp(log-lik − best), so points near the log-lik peak are larger. The fitted I_ref inferred from the slope is annotated — it should fall in the characteristic I range during epidemics (a few hundred to a few thousand)."
#| label: fig-ridge-tradeoff
#| fig-height: 4.5
prof_true_path = os.path.join(VDIR, "validation", "profile_s0_true.tsv")
prof_ext_path  = os.path.join(VDIR, "validation", "profile_s0_true_ext.tsv")

if os.path.exists(prof_true_path):
    dfs = [pl.read_csv(prof_true_path, separator="\t", comment_prefix="#")]
    if os.path.exists(prof_ext_path):
        dfs.append(pl.read_csv(prof_ext_path, separator="\t", comment_prefix="#"))
    prof = pl.concat(dfs).sort("s0")

    s0v = prof["s0"].to_numpy()
    alpha = prof["alpha"].to_numpy()
    ll = prof["max_loglik"].to_numpy()
    best_ll = ll.max()
    # Dot size ∝ exp((ll-best)/50) — points far below best become small
    weights = np.exp((ll - best_ll) / 50.0)
    sizes = 30 + 500 * weights / weights.max()

    # Fit line to ridge-active region: s0 > 0.05, where the trend is clear
    mask = s0v > 0.05
    xr = np.log10(s0v[mask])
    yr = alpha[mask]
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(xr, yr, 1)
    # dα/d(log10 s0) = slope → d(log s0)/dα = -ln(10)/slope
    # log I_ref = -d(log s0)/dα = ln(10)/slope
    log_Iref = np.log(10) / -slope   # sign convention: -log(I_ref)
    Iref = np.exp(log_Iref)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
    sc = ax.scatter(np.log10(s0v), alpha, s=sizes, c=ll, cmap="viridis_r",
                    edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
    # Theory line over full x-range
    x_line = np.linspace(np.log10(s0v.min()), np.log10(s0v.max()), 100)
    y_line = intercept + slope * x_line
    ax.plot(x_line, y_line, color="black", linewidth=1.2,
            label=f"fitted ridge (slope {slope:.2f})")
    # Truth point
    ax.scatter([np.log10(0.0297)], [0.976], marker="x", color="black",
                s=100, linewidth=2.2, zorder=10, label="truth (s0=0.030, α=0.976)")

    ax.annotate(
        f"slope $d\\alpha / d(\\log_{{10}} s_0) = {slope:.2f}$\n"
        f"⇒  $I_{{\\mathrm{{ref}}}} = \\exp({log_Iref:.1f}) \\approx {Iref:.0f}$",
        xy=(0.02, 0.05), xycoords="axes fraction", fontsize=11,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc="white", ec=GREY, alpha=0.85))

    ax.set_xlabel("log₁₀(s0)")
    ax.set_ylabel("α (mixing exponent)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    cb = plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, pad=0.02)
    cb.set_label("profile log-likelihood", fontsize=9)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

The inferred $I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (≈ 12,000 with the full grid including
extension to s₀ = 0.95) is a log-weighted mean of the infectious
population along the likelihood-dominant portions of the time series.
Physically this corresponds to the **peak infectious population during
a large epidemic**: London's weekly reported case count peaks at ~4000
cases, which with $\rho = 0.488$ gives ~8000 true weekly infections;
with an infectious period of ~12 days this is an instantaneous $I$ at
peak of ~14,000. The ridge is dominated by the peak because that's
where the likelihood signal is strongest — the model-observation match
at epidemic peaks drives the bulk of $\ell(\theta)$, not the troughs or
growth phases. Fitting over a narrower s₀ range (e.g. 0.05–0.3)
returns a smaller $I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (~800) corresponding to the
growth-phase infectious population, which is the scale that dominates
*locally* there. Both answers are self-consistent within the FOI
approximation; they weight the trajectory differently.

### Does this suggest a clean reparameterization?

The answer is **"partially, and pragmatically yes"**, with important
caveats.

The ridge-aligned coordinate is
$\kappa = \log s_0 + \alpha \log I_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and the orthogonal
direction $\nu$ (perpendicular to the ridge in the same 2D subspace)
is the non-identified direction. A *perfect* reparameterization would
fit $\kappa$ and place a strong prior on $\nu$, and the likelihood would
become identifiable in the new coordinates.

But three complications prevent this from being a *clean* algebraic
rotation of the parameter space:

1. **$I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is emergent, not a model parameter.** It depends
   on the data and on the full trajectory, so any reparameterization
   involving $I_{\mathrm{ref}}$ has to estimate it from the data too —
   making the new coordinates non-algebraic.

2. **The ridge is not purely 2D.** The profile figure shows $R_0$, γ, and
   amplitude also compensating (noisily) with s0. The full identifiable
   submanifold is higher-dimensional; the $(s_0, \alpha)$ rotation only
   captures its strongest axis.

3. **$\iota$ matters in troughs.** The derivation dropped $\iota$,
   which is valid during epidemics but not in the inter-epidemic
   troughs where $I$ dips near zero and $\iota$ dominates the FOI. The
   ridge slope changes there, complicating a global reparameterization.

The **pragmatic workaround**, and what the epidemiology literature has
converged on, is to **fix $\alpha$ at a biologically-informed value**
from the measles literature (He et al.'s $\alpha = 0.976$; other
pre-vaccination measles analyses put $\alpha$ at 0.95–1.0). This
effectively projects onto the ridge and eliminates one dimension of
ambiguity. The cost is that we no longer "let the data decide" $\alpha$
— but the data can't decide $\alpha$ from a 21-year London time series
in any case (as this analysis demonstrates), so nothing is lost.

An alternative that preserves more flexibility: put a **weakly
informative prior on $\alpha$** centered at 1 (the linear-mixing
reference) with small variance. This lets $\alpha$ adjust under strong
evidence but keeps it from drifting into the ridge's long tail. This is
the approach Gelman, Simpson, and Betancourt (2017) argue is generally
preferable to hard parameter fixing, since it reduces identifying
information coming from "the prior is a delta function" to "the prior
is concentrated."

The full identifiable combination from our model — the one that
*every* analysis can estimate robustly — is approximately the **early
epidemic growth rate** $r$, which satisfies
$r \approx \sigma \gamma s_0 (I^\alpha / I) / (\sigma + \gamma)$
and pins down a particular function of $(s_0, R_0, \alpha, \sigma, \gamma)$
rather than any individual parameter. If we fit $r$ first (from
pre-peak data, using e.g. a log-linear regression) and then use it as a
constraint in the full fit, we break the ridge at its structural source
rather than by parameter fiat.


## A second ridge: 2D profile over (R₀, γ)

Fixing $s_0$ at the profile peak breaks the $(s_0, \alpha)$ ridge but
leaves $R_0$ and $\gamma$ systematically biased (the fixed-s0 scout
below finds R₀ ≈ 74 vs truth 57, γ ≈ 0.15 vs truth 0.083). The profile
likelihood over $s_0$ already hinted at this: even at $s_0 = $ truth,
the conditional MLE of γ sits at ~0.16, never near truth. That
suggests a **second identifiability ridge** between $R_0$ and $\gamma$,
logically plausible because both enter transmission through $\beta =
R_0 \cdot (\gamma + \mu)$ and the observed epidemic shape depends on
their combination more than either individually.

We test this directly with a 2D profile: sweep $(R_0, \gamma)$ on a
14×14 grid, fix $s_0 = 0.025$, re-optimize the other three parameters
($\sigma, \alpha, \mathrm{amplitude}$) at each grid point via IF2.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "2D profile log-likelihood over (R₀, γ) with s₀ fixed at 0.025 and the other three parameters (σ, α, amplitude) re-optimized via IF2 at each grid point. Colormap: log-lik relative to the maximum. Contours at (−1, −5, −20, −100) nats below peak. Black X: truth (R₀=56.8, γ=0.083). Purple diamond: fixed-s0 scout MLE (R₀=73.7, γ=0.148). If there is a clean ridge coupling R₀ and γ, we should see a diagonal valley/plateau connecting truth and the scout MLE."
#| label: fig-profile-r0-gamma
#| fig-height: 6
prof2d_path = os.path.join(VDIR, "validation", "profile_r0_gamma.tsv")
if os.path.exists(prof2d_path):
    p2 = pl.read_csv(prof2d_path, separator="\t", comment_prefix="#")
    # Expected columns: R0, gamma, max_loglik, sigma, alpha, amplitude
    R0_vals = sorted(p2["R0"].unique())
    gamma_vals = sorted(p2["gamma"].unique())
    # Build log-lik grid (row = gamma, col = R0 for imshow convention)
    ll_grid = np.full((len(gamma_vals), len(R0_vals)), np.nan)
    for row in p2.iter_rows(named=True):
        i = gamma_vals.index(row["gamma"])
        j = R0_vals.index(row["R0"])
        ll_grid[i, j] = row["max_loglik"]
    best_ll = np.nanmax(ll_grid)
    delta = ll_grid - best_ll

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    im = ax.pcolormesh(R0_vals, gamma_vals, delta,
                       shading="auto", cmap="viridis",
                       vmin=-100, vmax=0)
    # Contours
    levels = [-100, -20, -5, -1]
    cs = ax.contour(R0_vals, gamma_vals, delta, levels=levels,
                    colors="white", linewidths=0.8, alpha=0.7)
    ax.clabel(cs, inline=True, fontsize=8, fmt="%d")
    # Truth + MLE markers
    ax.scatter([56.8], [0.0832], marker="x", color="black", s=140,
               linewidth=2.5, zorder=10, label="truth")
    ax.scatter([73.7], [0.1478], marker="D", color="#9333ea", s=80,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.0, zorder=10,
               label="fixed-s0 scout MLE")
    ax.set_xlabel("R₀")
    ax.set_ylabel("γ (recovery rate)")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=10)
    cb = plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, pad=0.02)
    cb.set_label("Δ log-likelihood (from peak)", fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    from IPython.display import Markdown
    display(Markdown("::: {.callout-note}\n## 2D profile pending\n"
                     "Running. Expected ~2.5 h. Re-render after "
                     "`validation/profile_r0_gamma.tsv` exists.\n:::"))
```

If a ridge is present, the iso-likelihood contours should form a
**diagonal valley** running from low-R₀/low-γ to high-R₀/high-γ
(positive correlation), because lowering γ lengthens the infectious
period and lowering R₀ compensates by reducing per-infectious-day
transmission so that the effective transmission over the infectious
period stays roughly constant. Truth and the scout MLE should both sit
*on* this ridge.


## Refitting with s0 fixed at the profile peak

The analytical derivation above says the $(s_0, \alpha)$ ridge makes
one of the two parameters redundant: the data identifies the combination
$\kappa = \log s_0 + \alpha \log I_{\mathrm{ref}}$, not $s_0$ and $\alpha$
separately. The pragmatic workaround — recommended in the measles
literature — is to fix one parameter (typically $\alpha$ from the
literature) and let the other absorb the identifiable information.

We do the inverse here: **fix $s_0$ at the profile-likelihood peak
($s_0 = 0.025$)** and re-estimate the remaining five parameters. Two
reasons to prefer fixing $s_0$ over fixing $\alpha$ for this chapter:

1. The profile peak is the value the *data* prefers (under the "everything
   else at conditional MLE" assumption). Fixing at the data-derived
   profile peak is self-consistent in a way that fixing $\alpha$ at
   `0.976 from He et al. 2010` is not — the latter brings in external
   prior information.
2. It demonstrates that the ridge can be broken from *either* side. The
   specific choice of which parameter to pin is a modeling decision,
   not a property of the data.

`fit_synthetic_fixed_s0.toml` has `s0 = 0.025` in the `[fixed]` block
and estimates only `R0, sigma, gamma, amplitude, alpha`:

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Comparing fit quality in decibans

Log-likelihood *differences* are the natural unit for comparing competing
fits: $\Delta \ell$ nats = $\log$ of the posterior odds (under a flat
prior) between two parameter settings. Converting to decibans
($1 \text{ dB} = 10 \log_{10}(\text{odds ratio})$, Turing's
weight-of-evidence unit) makes the scale human-interpretable.

| scout config | ll spread across chains | in decibans | odds ratio best:worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6-param scout (s0 estimated) | ~18,000 nats | **~78,000 dB** | $10^{7800}$ |
| 5-param scout (s0 fixed at profile peak) | 119 nats | **~520 dB** | $10^{52}$ |

(*) Updated after the fixed-s0 scout completes.

The deciban framing exposes what Â — uniformly near 1.00 on all the
6-param scouts — was hiding: chains occupied parameter basins differing
in likelihood by tens of thousands of decibans. Fixing s0 at the profile
peak collapses this "meta-model uncertainty" (fitting-procedure
ambiguity about which basin is best) by roughly **three orders of
magnitude on the log-scale of log-likelihood**. The remaining
within-basin spread represents Monte-Carlo variance in IF2 convergence,
not genuine basin disagreement.

In practice, for scouts at scale: *how many decibans of evidence
separate your best and worst chains?* If it's in the hundreds-to-
thousands range, your scout is finding qualitatively different answers
— you have a multimodality problem regardless of what Â says. If
it's under ~30 dB (odds ratio $< 10^3$), chains are in the same
neighborhood and disagreement is numerical noise.
:::

```{python}
display(run_cli(
    f"cat {VDIR}/fit_synthetic_fixed_s0.toml",
    echo="cat fit_synthetic_fixed_s0.toml",
    collapse=True, max_lines=None,
))

```{python}
#| echo: false
def _fixed_s0_scout_dir():
    """Find the fixed-s0 scout dir (output_dir='results/synthetic_fixed_s0').
    Its results tree follows the same fit_synthetic_fixed_s0-<hash>/
    convention as the other runs."""
    matches = glob.glob(os.path.join(
        VDIR, "results/fits/fit_synthetic_fixed_s0-*/real/fit_42/scout"))
    populated = [p for p in matches
                 if os.path.exists(os.path.join(p, "fit_state.toml"))]
    if not populated:
        return None
    populated.sort(key=lambda p: os.path.getmtime(
        os.path.join(p, "fit_state.toml")))
    return populated[-1]

SCOUT_FIXED_DIR = _fixed_s0_scout_dir()
scout_fixed_populated = (SCOUT_FIXED_DIR is not None
                          and os.path.exists(
                              os.path.join(SCOUT_FIXED_DIR, "fit_state.toml")))
```

if scout_fixed_populated:

    chain_dirs_fx = [p for p in glob.glob(
        os.path.join(SCOUT_FIXED_DIR, "chain_*")) if os.path.isdir(p)]
    for cdir in sorted(chain_dirs_fx,

                         separator="\t", infer_schema_length=10000)
        cid = int(os.path.basename(cdir).split("_")[1])
        df = df.with_columns(pl.lit(cid).alias("chain"))
        traces_fx.append(df)
    traces_fx_df = pl.concat(traces_fx) if traces_fx else None

    with open(os.path.join(SCOUT_FIXED_DIR, "fit_state.toml"), "rb") as f:
        state_fx = tomllib.load(f)
    chain_lls_fx = state_fx.get("chain_logliks", [])
    agreements_fx = state_fx.get("tail_chain_agreement", {})
    with open(os.path.join(SCOUT_FIXED_DIR, "mle_params.toml"), "rb") as f:
        mle_fx = tomllib.load(f)
else:
    traces_fx_df = None
    chain_lls_fx, agreements_fx, mle_fx = [], {}, {}

    good_threshold = best - 500
    colors = ["#3366cc" if ll > good_threshold else "#cc3333"
              for ll in sorted_lls]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.2))
    ax.bar(range(len(sorted_lls)), sorted_lls, color=colors, edgecolor="none")
    ax.axhline(best, color=GREY, linewidth=0.5, linestyle=":",
               label=f"best = {best:.1f}")
    n_good = sum(1 for ll in chain_lls_fx if ll > good_threshold)
    n_bad = len(chain_lls_fx) - n_good
    subtitle = (f"{n_good}/{len(chain_lls_fx)} chains within 500 nats of best"
                + (f" · {n_bad} diverged" if n_bad else " · no divergences"))
    ax.set_title(subtitle, fontsize=10, color=GREY)
    ax.set_xlabel("Chain (sorted)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Final log-likelihood")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    print("| parameter | truth | MLE (best chain) | Â | % error | status |")

    for p in params_est:
        truth = TRUE_PARAMS[p]

        pct_err = 100 * abs(mle - truth) / abs(truth) if truth != 0 else float("nan")
        if agreement < 1.05 and pct_err < 10:
            status = "✓ converged + recovered"
        elif agreement < 1.05 and pct_err < 20:
            status = "✓ converged + near-truth"
        elif agreement < 1.05:
            status = "⚠ converged but biased"
        elif agreement < 1.10:
            status = "~ marginal"
        else:
            status = "✗ not converged"
        print(f"| `{p}` | {truth:.4g} | {mle:.4g} | {agreement:.3f} "
              f"| {pct_err:.1f}% | {status} |")

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Pair plot for the fixed-s0 scout, 5 estimated parameters. **Red dots** = pre-cooled iterations 1–50 (all chains) showing where IF2 explored before the cooling schedule pulled chains inward. **Blue dots on top** = converged iterations 140–200 showing where chains settled. Rings = per-chain MLEs from `final_params.toml`. Truth X marks truth values. No s0 panel (it's fixed at 0.025). The red exploration cloud sits wider than the blue converged cluster and traces out the identifiability ridges visually — compare the (R₀, γ) panel especially, where the red cloud elongates along a diagonal that's a direct visualization of the likelihood ridge, while blue has collapsed to a single point."
#| label: fig-pair-plot-fixed
#| fig-height: 8.5
if scout_fixed_populated and traces_fx_df is not None:
    params_est = ["R0", "sigma", "gamma", "amplitude", "alpha"]
    N_LAST = 60
    N_EARLY = 50   # pre-cooled iterations
    max_iter = int(traces_fx_df["iteration"].max())
    tail_df = traces_fx_df.filter(pl.col("iteration") > max_iter - N_LAST)
    early_df = traces_fx_df.filter(pl.col("iteration") < N_EARLY)

    endpoints_rows = []
    for cid in sorted(traces_fx_df["chain"].unique()):
        fp_path = os.path.join(SCOUT_FIXED_DIR, f"chain_{cid}", "final_params.toml")
        if not os.path.exists(fp_path):
            continue
        with open(fp_path, "rb") as f:
            fp = tomllib.load(f)
        row = {"chain": int(cid)}
        for p in params_est:
            row[p] = fp.get(p, float("nan"))
        endpoints_rows.append(row)
    endpoints = pl.DataFrame(endpoints_rows).sort("chain")

    chain_ll_map = {cid: ll for cid, ll in enumerate(chain_lls_fx, start=1)}
    best_ll = max(chain_lls_fx)

    def _basin(ll):
        if ll > best_ll - 500:   return 0
        if ll > best_ll - 2000:  return 1
        if ll > best_ll - 6000:  return 2
        return 3

    basin_colors = {0: "#1e3a8a", 1: "#f59e0b", 2: "#9333ea", 3: "#cc3333"}
    basin_labels = {0: "best (<500 nats)", 1: "middle (500–2000)",
                    2: "middle (2000–6000)", 3: "worst (>6000)"}

    tail_rows = tail_df.to_dicts()
    tail_basin = np.array([_basin(chain_ll_map[r["chain"]]) for r in tail_rows])
    tail_arr = {p: np.array([r[p] for r in tail_rows]) for p in params_est}

    early_rows = early_df.to_dicts()
    early_arr = {p: np.array([r[p] for r in early_rows]) for p in params_est}

    ep_basin = [_basin(chain_ll_map[c]) for c in endpoints["chain"].to_list()]
    ep_x = {p: endpoints[p].to_numpy() for p in params_est}

    n = len(params_est)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n, n, figsize=(12, 8.5))
    for i, py in enumerate(params_est):
        for j, px in enumerate(params_est):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            if i == j:
                # Diagonal: hist of converged-phase values (on top of hist of
                # early values in light red for context)
                if len(early_arr[py]):
                    ax.hist(early_arr[py], bins=25, color="#cc3333",
                            alpha=0.30, edgecolor="none")
                for b in sorted(set(tail_basin)):
                    vals = tail_arr[py][tail_basin == b]
                    if len(vals):
                        ax.hist(vals, bins=25, color=basin_colors[b],
                                alpha=0.70, edgecolor="none")
                ax.axvline(TRUE_PARAMS[py], color="black", linewidth=1.2,
                           linestyle="--", alpha=0.85)
                ax.set_yticks([])
            else:
                # Pre-cooled exploration cloud (background, red)
                if len(early_arr[px]) and len(early_arr[py]):
                    ax.scatter(early_arr[px], early_arr[py],
                               color="#cc3333", alpha=0.12, s=4, linewidth=0,
                               zorder=1)
                # Converged cloud (foreground, basin-colored)
                for b in sorted(set(tail_basin)):
                    m = tail_basin == b
                    if m.any():
                        ax.scatter(tail_arr[px][m], tail_arr[py][m],
                                   color=basin_colors[b], alpha=0.35,
                                   s=5, linewidth=0, zorder=3)
                for b in sorted(set(ep_basin)):
                    mask = [k for k in range(len(ep_basin)) if ep_basin[k] == b]
                    if mask:
                        ax.scatter([ep_x[px][k] for k in mask],
                                   [ep_x[py][k] for k in mask],
                                   facecolors="none", edgecolors=basin_colors[b],
                                   s=60, linewidth=1.2, zorder=6)
                ax.scatter(TRUE_PARAMS[px], TRUE_PARAMS[py],
                           marker="x", color="black", s=90, linewidth=2.2,
                           zorder=10)
            if i == n - 1: ax.set_xlabel(px, fontsize=10)
            else:          ax.set_xticklabels([])
            if j == 0:     ax.set_ylabel(py, fontsize=10)
            else:          ax.set_yticklabels([])
            ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
            ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    handles = [plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w",
                           markerfacecolor="#cc3333", markersize=8,
                           alpha=0.4, label="pre-cooled (iter 1-50)")]
    handles += [plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w",
                           markerfacecolor=basin_colors[b], markersize=8,
                           label=f"converged · {basin_labels[b]}")
                for b in sorted(set(ep_basin))]
    handles.append(plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w",
                               markerfacecolor="none", markeredgecolor="black",
                               markeredgewidth=1.2, markersize=9,
                               label="per-chain MLE"))
    handles.append(plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="x", color="black",
                               linewidth=0, markersize=9, label="truth"))
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="center left",
                bbox_to_anchor=(0.82, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 0.80, 1))
    plt.show()
